sections.title: Feed Your Mind — Books, Movies, Speeches and Lifelong Learning

blocks.html: Start here Your body becomes what you eat. Your mind is the same. It becomes what you read, watch, hear, and the people you spend time with. So choose your mind’s “food” with care.
blocks.text:
Start here Your body becomes what you eat. Your mind
is the same. It becomes what you read, watch, hear , and
the people you spend time with. So choose your mind’s
“food” with care.

blocks.caption:
Books, films, music and people all
flow into the person you become.

blocks.html: “You are the books you read, the movies you watch, the music you listen to, the people you spend time with, the conversations you engage in. Choose wisely what you feed your mind.”
blocks.text:
“You are the books you read, the movies you watch, the music you
listen to, the people you spend time with, the conversations you engage
in. Choose wisely what you feed your mind.”

blocks.html: We can’t always pick our surroundings. But most of the time we do have a choice, so pick places and people that help you grow.

The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People Stephen Covey Win inside yourself first, then win in the world outside.

One Minute for Yourself Spencer Johnson Make time for your own happiness before trying to make others happy.
Steal Like an Artist Austin Kleon Nothing is fully original. Copy your heroes, give them credit, practise, and your own style grows.
Thrive Arianna Huffington Success is not only productivity. Well-being and wisdom matter too.

Movies with life lessons

blocks.html:
Movie Lesson
The Karate Kid A skill is for self-protection, not showing off. Avoid fights first.
Kung Fu Panda A funny film full of wisdom. Po the panda finds the power already inside him.
The Lion King Simba loses belief after his father dies. Friends help him find himself again.
Groundhog Day The same day repeats again and again. When he changes his attitude and starts helping people, his life moves forward.
Forrest Gump Keep going, whatever happens: persistence and self-belief.

blocks.html:
Lecture example — four ways to solve a conflict The teacher links The Karate Kid to an old Indian idea: sama, dana, bheda, danda.

  1. Sama: talk it out peacefully.
  2. Dana: give something in return.
  3. Bheda: split the other side.
  4. Danda: fight, only if nothing else works. This works for arguments at work too, not just physical fights.

Be a lifelong learner, and a
mentor

blocks.alt: Learn and teach, all life long
blocks.caption:
Learn from everyone around
you, and teach what you know. Both make you grow.

blocks.html:
• Learning doesn’t stop at Class 12 or graduation.
  • We learn from books, films and speeches, but most of all from people: everyday positive people around us, not just famous ones.
  • Nature and people around you are great teachers. Keep watching and learning.
  • Teach too. When you mentor someone, you learn from them as well. It’s “360-degree learning”.

sections.title: Use What You Learn — Ice Stupas, Theme Parks and Shoes

blocks.html: Start here High up in Ladakh, there is plenty of snow in winter. But in spring and early summer, when farmers need water, the streams are nearly dry. Hundreds of villages faced this. The answer came from a science lesson you learned in school.

The ice stupa

blocks.html: Ladakh is cold, dry and rocky. You can’t easily dig ponds or wells there. In summer some people even had to leave their villages for a few months.
blocks.text:
Ladakh is cold, dry and rocky . You can’t easily dig
ponds or wells there. In summer some people even had to leave their
villages for a few months.

blocks.html: The school science: a big block of ice melts slowly. A small piece melts fast. Why? A big block has less surface for its size, so it takes in heat more slowly. (That’s also why we spread hot food out to cool it faster.)
blocks.text:

blocks.html: Lecture example — the Ice House in Chennai Near Marina Beach stands a building once called the Ice House (today Vivekananda House). In the 1800s, huge blocks of ice came by ship all the way from America and were stored there. Big blocks lasted for months.
blocks.text:
Lecture example — the Ice House in Chennai Near
Marina Beach stands a building once called the Ice
House (today Vivekananda House ). In the 1800s,
huge blocks of ice came by ship all the way from
America and were stored there. Big blocks lasted for months.

blocks.html: The idea: engineer Sonam Wangchuk piped stream water up through a pipe so it sprayed out like a fountain in the freezing winter. The water froze layer by layer into a tall cone of ice, called an ice stupa. In spring and summer it melts slowly, giving water just when farms need it.

Two men at
Disney World: the entrepreneurial mindset

blocks.caption:
Same trip, different thinking:
one enjoys it, the other asks “What if we had this at home?”

blocks.html: Long ago, two men from India visited Disney World in the USA. Both loved it.
blocks.text:

blocks.html:
• The first came home and told everyone how much fun it was.
  • The second asked, “What if we had theme parks in our country? People who can’t travel to the USA could enjoy them too.” He went on to build theme parks in India.

sections.title: Failure, Fear and the Panic Button

blocks.html: Start here You have a class in 30 minutes. It’s raining hard. You park your car and see the back lights won’t switch off. The battery will drain! Your heart races. What do you do? The answer depends on whether you panic or pause.
blocks.text:
Start here You have a class in 30 minutes. It’s
raining hard. You park your car and see the back lights won’t switch
off. The battery will drain! Your heart races. What do you do? The
answer depends on whether you panic or pause .
Denial wastes time

blocks.html: Lecture example — the promotion that didn’t come A young professor was sure he’d be promoted. Everyone thought so. One of the interviewers was even his old friend. But he wasn’t promoted. He went into denial: “How can they pick others and not me?” He spoke badly of the people who were promoted, and even of his friend. A whole year passed with nothing done. He was promoted the next time, but that year was lost.
blocks.text:
Lecture example — the promotion that didn’t come A
young professor was sure he’d be promoted. Everyone thought so. One of
the interviewers was even his old friend. But he wasn’t
promoted . He went into denial : “How can they
pick others and not me?” He spoke badly of the people who were promoted,
and even of his friend. A whole year passed with
nothing done. He was promoted the next time, but that year was lost.

blocks.html: What should he have done? Accept it, find out what was missing, and prepare better.
blocks.text:
What should he have done? Accept it , find out what
was missing, and prepare better .

blocks.html: Know what’s in your control:
blocks.text: Know what’s in your control:

blocks.html:
• You control your preparation and effort.
  • You don’t control the result once it’s out of your hands.
  • If you’ve done your best, accept the result and learn from it.
blocks.text:
You control your preparation and effort . You don’t control the result once it’s out of your
hands. If you’ve done your best, accept the result and
learn from it.

blocks.html: Thomas Edison was asked about his many failed experiments for the light bulb. His idea: each one wasn’t a failure, it taught him one more material that didn’t work. Every failure brought success closer.
blocks.text:
Thomas Edison was asked about his many failed
experiments for the light bulb. His idea: each one wasn’t a failure, it taught him one more material that didn’t work . Every

Fear of failure

blocks.html: We worry: “What if I fail the exam? What if I don’t get promoted?” Too much worry stops us from trying and steals our joy.
blocks.text:
We worry: “What if I fail the exam? What if I don’t get promoted?”
Too much worry stops us from trying and steals our
joy.

blocks.html: Everyday example: fear of water can stop you learning to swim. Face it, and you gain a skill that could save your life one day.
blocks.text:
Everyday example: fear of water can stop you
learning to swim. Face it, and you gain a skill that could save
your life one day.

blocks.html:
• Take calculated risks, ones you can manage.
  • Don’t let one failure stay in your head. A cricket captain who keeps worrying about the last loss may lose the next match too.
blocks.text:
Take calculated risks , ones you can manage. Don’t let one failure stay in your head. A cricket captain who keeps
worrying about the last loss may lose the next match too.

The panic button: amygdala
hijack

blocks.html: When we panic, a small part of the brain called the amygdala takes over. The thinking part of the brain (the neocortex) switches off. We get only three choices:
blocks.text:
When we panic, a small part of the brain called the amygdala takes over. The thinking part of the brain
(the neocortex ) switches off. We get only three
choices:

blocks.html:
F What it looks like
Fight Argue, shout, attack
Flight Run away from the problem
Freeze Get stuck, do nothing
blocks.text: F What it looks like Fight Argue, shout, attack Flight Run away from the problem Freeze Get stuck, do nothing

blocks.html: This is called an amygdala hijack. Decisions made in panic are often poor ones.
blocks.text:
This is called an amygdala hijack . Decisions made in
panic are often poor ones.

blocks.caption:
In panic, the brain picks fight, flight or
freeze. A short pause lets the thinking brain come back.

blocks.text:
Three ways to keep
the panic button far away

blocks.caption:
Dry run, pause, and chess
move.

blocks.html:
Tool What you do Example
1. Dry run Practise the event before it happens, to catch problems early Rehearsing a big event (did we keep water for the guest?); solving mock papers before an exam
2. Pause Stop for a moment. Let your heartbeat slow down and let the thinking brain return. Works for panic, anxiety and anger
3. Chess move Like in chess, think about the next few moves: who might object, what could go wrong. Also ask: has this been done before? His old director always asked these two questions

blocks.html: Start here A guitar string that’s too loose makes no music. Too tight, and it snaps. Stress is the same. A little stretches you and helps you grow. Too much for too long breaks you down.
blocks.text:
Start here A guitar string that’s too loose makes no
music. Too tight, and it snaps. Stress is the same. A
little stretches you and helps you grow. Too much for
too long breaks you down.
What is stress?

blocks.html:
• Every system has a natural state of order and balance. When it is pushed away from that state, we feel stress.
  • We are made of mind, body and brain, all connected. Stress in one part spreads to the others.
  • We are also part of a bigger system: people, nature, the world. So stress can come from inside us or outside us.
  • Some stress is good. It pushes you out of your comfort zone.
  • Too much, for too long, hurts your health, self-worth and performance.
  • So treat the root cause, not just the symptoms.
blocks.text:
Every system has a natural state of order and
balance . When it is pushed away from that
state, we feel stress . We are made of mind, body and brain , all connected.
Stress in one part spreads to the others. We are also part of a bigger system : people,
nature, the world. So stress can come from inside us or outside us. Some stress is good. It pushes you out of your
comfort zone. Too much, for too long, hurts your health,
self-worth and performance. So treat the root cause , not just the
symptoms.
Three ways to manage stress

blocks.html:
1. Manage your energy (this page)
  2. Manage your time (next page)
  3. Build rituals that join good habits together (next page)
blocks.text:
Manage your energy (this page) Manage your time (next page) Build rituals that join good habits together (next
page)

Nine practices to manage
your energy

blocks.caption:
Sleep, body clock, movement, food,
breath, meditation, journaling, gratitude and kindness all fill your
energy.

blocks.html:
Practice What to do Why it helps
1. Follow your body clock Sleep, wake and eat at regular times, in step with sunrise and sunset Your body has a 24-hour clock (the circadian rhythm). Working with it is like rowing downstream.
2. Sleep well Enough deep sleep at regular times. The teacher suggests bed by about 10 pm. The body repairs itself. The brain stores what you learned into long-term memory.
3. Move and exercise Regular activity More energy and stamina; better blood flow; a healthier brain that keeps learning at any age
4. Eat well Fresh, seasonal, local food; less packaged and junk food; regular meal times; chew well, no phone while eating Food is fuel. Stress while eating disturbs digestion.
5. Breathe deeply Breathe slowly into your belly, then breathe out fully, a few times a day Calms you, clears your mind, boosts focus
6. Meditate 10–15 minutes daily; watch your thoughts without fighting them Clear, calm mind; better focus and creativity
7. Journal Write whatever comes to mind, every day (morning or bedtime) Clears the mind, reduces overthinking, helps you understand your feelings
8. Be grateful Think about what you are, have and can do, not what you lack Shifts your energy instantly; reminds you of your strengths
9. Be kind Be kind to others, and first to yourself Releases “feel-good” chemicals (oxytocin, serotonin). Even watching kindness lifts you.

How to meditate: the muddy
water

blocks.html: Lecture example — the jar of muddy water The Buddha shook a jar of muddy water. It stayed cloudy while he kept shaking it. When he set it down, the mud slowly settled and the water became clear. Our mind is the same. Fighting our thoughts stirs them up. Leave them alone and they settle.
blocks.text:
Lecture example — the jar of muddy water The Buddha
shook a jar of muddy water. It stayed cloudy while he kept shaking it.
When he set it down , the mud slowly settled and the water became clear. Our mind is the
same. Fighting our thoughts stirs them up. Leave them
alone and they settle.

blocks.caption:
Stop shaking the jar and the mud
settles. Stop fighting your thoughts and the mind clears.

blocks.html: The key: be an observer. Imagine sitting on a balcony watching clouds pass by. Do the same with your thoughts:
blocks.text:
The key: be an observer. Imagine sitting on a
balcony watching clouds pass by . Do the same with your
thoughts:

blocks.html:
• No judging: not “good thought” or “bad thought”.
  • No holding on: don’t chase the nice thoughts.
  • No pushing away: don’t fight the unpleasant ones.
blocks.text:
No judging : not “good thought” or “bad
thought”. No holding on : don’t chase the nice thoughts. No pushing away : don’t fight the unpleasant
ones.

blocks.html: Thoughts won’t vanish on day 1. Like any habit, it takes daily practice.
blocks.text: Thoughts won’t vanish on day 1. Like any habit, it takes daily practice .
Journaling tip

blocks.html: Don’t know what to write? Write “I don’t know what to write” again and again. Soon your pen takes over. There’s no right or wrong way. It’s your safe, private space.
blocks.text:

sections.title: Manage Your Time and Build Rituals

blocks.html: Start here Everyone gets the same 24 hours, the toppers and the people who are always late. The difference isn’t how much time they have. It’s how they plan, choose and use it.
blocks.text:
Start here Everyone gets the same 24 hours, the
toppers and the people who are always late. The difference isn’t how
much time they have. It’s how they plan, choose and use
it .
The six P’s of time

blocks.html:
P What it means
1. Big Picture What do you really want in 3, 5 or 10 years? What kind of person do you want to become? What are your values?
2. Prepare Make weekly and daily task lists. Estimate the time each task needs. Set deadlines.
3. Prioritise Decide what matters most: the Eisenhower matrix, the 80/20 rule, and learning to say no.
4. Plan Put tasks on your calendar at the right times of day. Add breaks, a little distraction time and some buffer time.
5. Be Productive Be consistent. Cut distractions, beat procrastination, don’t multitask.
6. Perform Just start. Progress, not perfection. Focus on the process.
blocks.text:
P What it means 1. Big Picture What do you really want in 3, 5 or 10 years? What kind of person do you want to become? What are your values ? 2. Prepare Make weekly and daily task lists . Estimate the time
each task needs. Set deadlines. 3. Prioritise Decide what matters most: the Eisenhower matrix, the 80/20 rule, and
learning to say no . 4. Plan Put tasks on your calendar at the right times of day. Add breaks, a
little distraction time and some buffer time. 5. Be Productive Be consistent. Cut distractions, beat
procrastination, don’t multitask. 6. Perform Just start. Progress, not perfection. Focus on the
process.
Why write a task list?

blocks.html:
• Tasks stop swimming around in your head, so your mind feels lighter.
  • You sleep better if you list tomorrow’s tasks before bed.
  • You don’t waste the morning figuring out what to do.
blocks.text:
Tasks stop swimming around in your head, so your mind feels lighter . You sleep better if you list tomorrow’s tasks
before bed. You don’t waste the morning figuring out what to do.

blocks.html: Sort tasks into big (hard, need full focus), medium (regular work) and small (easy, quick). Use paper, Google Calendar, Notion or any app.
blocks.text:
Sort tasks into big (hard, need full focus), medium (regular work) and small (easy,
quick). Use paper, Google Calendar, Notion or any app.

Prioritise with the
Eisenhower matrix

blocks.caption:
Sort every task by “urgent?” and
“important?”, then act.

blocks.html:
Urgent Not urgent
Important 1. Do it now: deadlines, emergencies 2. Schedule it: health, study, family, hobbies. Do these regularly so they don’t become urgent.
Not important 3. Delegate or automate: hand it off, use an app 4. Delete it: time-wasters, mindless scrolling
blocks.text:
Urgent Not urgent Important 1. Do it now : deadlines, emergencies 2. Schedule it : health, study, family, hobbies. Do
these regularly so they don’t become urgent. Not important 3. Delegate or automate : hand it off, use an
app 4. Delete it : time-wasters, mindless scrolling

blocks.html: Stephen Covey made this matrix popular, so it’s also called the Covey matrix.
blocks.text: Stephen Covey made this matrix popular, so it’s also called the Covey matrix .

The 80/20 rule (Pareto
principle)

blocks.html: About 20% of your efforts give 80% of your results. Find that 20% and spend most of your time there.
blocks.text:
About 20% of your efforts give 80% of your
results . Find that 20% and spend most of your time there.

blocks.html:
• Study: focus first on the key concepts that give most of the marks.
  • Habits: find the 1–3 habits that help you most and strengthen them. Find the 1–3 that hurt you most and drop them.
blocks.text:
Study: focus first on the key concepts that give
most of the marks. Habits: find the 1–3 habits that help you most and strengthen them. Find the 1–3 that hurt you most and drop them.
Learn to say no

blocks.html: Saying no to some things lets you say yes to what matters. Make a checklist.
blocks.text: Saying no to some things lets you say yes to what matters. Make a checklist.

blocks.html:
Say yes if… Say no if…
It’s important or urgent (deadlines, assignments) You’re only saying yes out of fear of missing out or peer pressure
It matches your goals and values You’re trying to please or impress others
It’s a healthy, productive habit It’s only instant fun with no real gain
It energises and inspires you It drains you or makes you act like someone you’re not

Plan your day: the 1-3-5 rule

blocks.caption:
One big task when your energy is highest,
three medium ones, five small ones when energy is low.

blocks.html: Each day, pick 1 big task, 3 medium tasks and 5 small tasks.
blocks.text: Each day, pick 1 big task, 3 medium tasks and 5 small tasks.

blocks.html:
• High energy time → the big task
  • Medium energy → medium tasks, grouped together
  • Low energy → small, routine tasks, grouped together
blocks.text:
High energy time → the big task Medium energy → medium tasks,
grouped together Low energy → small , routine tasks,
grouped together

blocks.html: Consistency is key: get 1% better every day and in a year you’re about 37 times better (1.01³⁶⁵ ≈ 37.8).
blocks.text:
Consistency is key: get 1% better every
day and in a year you’re about 37 times better
(1.01³⁶⁵ ≈ 37.8).
Build rituals

blocks.html: A ritual is a routine done on purpose, with full attention, because you know its value. It need not be religious.
blocks.text:
A ritual is a routine done on purpose, with
full attention , because you know its value. It need not be
religious.

blocks.html:
Habit Ritual
Done because you’re used to it Done because you want to and know why
Mind elsewhere Fully present, calm, enjoying each step
blocks.text: Habit Ritual Done because you’re used to it Done because you want to and know why Mind elsewhere Fully present , calm, enjoying each step

blocks.html: How to build one:
blocks.text: How to build one:

blocks.html:
1. Pick the routine (morning, study, sleep, exercise, journaling…).
  2. Write down why it matters, and stick the note where you can see it.
  3. List the steps.
  4. Gather what you need, and fix the time and place.
  5. Set up the space so it puts you in the mood.
  6. Do it mindfully, keep it fun, and adjust as you go.
blocks.text:

you can see it. List the steps . Gather what you need, and fix the time and

blocks.html: Tiny changes → tiny gains → huge results over time. Spending 30–45 minutes on a wake-up ritual and a bedtime ritual can change a lot.

blocks.html: Start here Hotel receptionist. Travel agent. Computer salesman. Lawyer. IT consultant. Nature-inspired design expert. That’s one person’s career. A career doesn’t have to be a straight line, and every turn can teach you something.

Who is Prof. Shiva
Subramanian?

blocks.html: Biomimicry means copying nature’s clever solutions. If nature faced a problem like yours, find out how nature solved it and use the same idea.

Lesson 1: Don’t regret for
too long

blocks.html: His life had many setbacks, and the switch from law to TCS was a big one.
blocks.text:
His life had many setbacks, and the switch from law to TCS was a big
one.

blocks.html:
• It’s natural to feel bad after missing a job, a promotion or money.
  • Feel it for a while: stay home, watch films, read, meet friends.
  • Then get up and start again. Don’t spend years regretting.

Lesson 2: His view on
work-life balance

blocks.html: Prof. Shiva says that, when you’re young, you should give your work almost everything. Doing well at work is how you take care of your family.

blocks.html: Lecture example — the house loan He wanted a ₹10 lakh house. The company would lend only ₹3 lakh, and he had ₹2 lakh. Because he had worked hard for three years and everyone liked him, the HR head asked the chairman for ₹5 lakh more, and got it.

Lesson 4: Tips
for interviews and your first job

blocks.html: In the interview:
blocks.text: In the interview:

blocks.html:
• Talk about what you’re good at. Don’t worry about the gaps.
  • Employers want problem solvers. Solve a few real problems (a money problem at home, settling a fight between friends) and share one example.

blocks.html: In your first 3–4 years:
blocks.text: In your first 3–4 years:

blocks.html:
• Get involved: picnics, parties, events, training. Volunteer. He always offered to be the master of ceremonies, so everyone knew him.
  • Show your talent: singing, dancing, anything. Don’t be shy.
  • Help people: he drove colleagues to hospital and stayed with them.
  • Own problems. Try to solve them first. If you’re stuck, go to your manager with 2–3 possible solutions, not just the problem.
  • Act like an owner (an entrepreneur inside the company).

1. Learn to lead

Style Focus

2. Aim higher

blocks.alt: Aim higher: the bulb and its circle of light
blocks.caption:
The higher the
bulb, the wider the circle of light. Aim higher and you see

blocks.html:
• Success is a journey, not a destination. When you reach one goal, the next one appears.
  • The higher you rise, the higher the bar, and it can feel lonely at the top.
  • Start now: if you’re an assistant manager, try to understand your boss’s boss’s problems. You’ll see the bigger picture.
  • Goal-setting research (psychologist Edwin Locke, late 1960s): clear, specific and difficult goals, once accepted, lead to better performance than vague “do your best” goals.
  • Aiming high cuts out noise: less time on gossip, more on ideas.

3. Honesty is still the best
policy

blocks.html:
• Be honest with yourself and with the world.
  • Some offers look like lollipops: tempting now, trouble later. Don’t grab them.
  • Honest people sleep well. Nothing heavy sits on their mind. A lie needs more lies to cover it, and that keeps you awake at night.
  • Research on trust at work says honesty and openness are the biggest signs of integrity. Leaders who break their team’s trust end up with unhappy employees who want to leave.

Failure, fear and panic

blocks.html:
• Denial wastes time. Accept what you can’t control and learn from it.
  • Edison: every failed try teaches you something.
  • Fear of failure stops you from trying. Take calculated risks.
  • Amygdala hijack → fight, flight or freeze.
  • Anti-panic tools: dry run, pause, chess move.
blocks.text:
Denial wastes time. Accept what you can’t control
and learn from it. Edison: every failed try teaches you
something. Fear of failure stops you from trying. Take calculated
risks . Amygdala hijack → fight, flight or freeze. Anti-panic tools: dry run , pause , chess move .
Manage stress

blocks.html:
• A little stress helps; too much for too long harms. Treat the root cause.
  • Energy: body clock, sleep, exercise, food, deep breathing, meditation (just observe), journaling, gratitude, kindness.
  • Time, the six P’s: Big picture, Prepare, Prioritise, Plan, Be productive, Perform.
  • Eisenhower: do now, schedule, delegate, delete. 80/20 rule. Learn to say no. 1-3-5 rule.
  • Rituals: routines done mindfully and on purpose.

Career advice (Prof. Shiva)

blocks.html:
• Don’t regret for too long.
  • Integrity: do it right when no one is watching (Madhava).
  • Be a problem solver; take 2–3 options to your manager.
  • Get involved in your first years; act like an owner.

Closing advice

blocks.html:
• Lead: care for people; character is most of leadership.
  • Aim higher: success is a journey; specific, hard goals (Locke).
  • Stay honest; read between the lines; help India grow.
